title: Board the USS Alabama at Mobile Bay
description: A South Dakota-class battleship that earned nine battle stars and was saved by Alabama schoolchildren collecting coins in 1964.

title: Walk Kelly Ingram Park and the Civil Rights Institute
description: The park where police turned dogs and hoses on schoolchildren in 1963, across the road from the church where four girls were killed that September.

title: Swim the falls at Little River Canyon
description: One of the few rivers in the country that runs its whole length on top of a mountain, cutting a gorge 200 metres deep. Free.

title: Watch the spring bird fallout on Dauphin Island
description: First land after a 900km Gulf crossing, so an April storm can drop thousands of exhausted songbirds into a few hectares of scrub.

title: Stand outside Little Rock Central High
description: Still a working school. Nine students walked in past a mob and the National Guard in 1957; the visitor centre opposite tells it plainly.

title: See the American art at Crystal Bridges
description: Safdie pavilions built over a ravine, holding American art from colonial portraits to Rothko, and free to enter permanently.

title: Walk to Hawksbill Crag
description: A cantilevered stone beak over the Buffalo River valley, five kilometres return down a forest road most hire cars will manage in the dry.

title: Walk the whole town of Eureka Springs
description: A Victorian spa town built into a hillside so steep no street crosses another at a right angle, and the whole of it is on the historic register.

title: Drive to the highest point in Arkansas
description: Eight hundred and thirty-nine metres, with hang gliders launching off the south bluff and black bear in the woods below.

title: Walk the memorials after dark
description: Lincoln, Korea and Vietnam are open and lit all night, and are entirely different places without the daytime crowds. Free.

title: See the Library of Congress reading room
description: The largest library in the world by shelf length. The Great Hall is free; the reading room floor needs a reader card, which is also free.

title: Walk under the cherry trees before the crowds
description: Three thousand trees given by Tokyo in 1912. Peak bloom lasts about four days and is forecast weeks ahead; go at sunrise.

title: Eat a half-smoke at Ben's Chili Bowl
description: Open on U Street since 1958, through the 1968 riots and the years afterwards when almost nothing else on the street stayed open.

title: See the Hope Diamond and the whale at Natural History
place: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History
description: Free, like every Smithsonian, and big enough that picking two halls beats trying to see it all.

title: Float the Boise River through town
description: Ten kilometres from Barber Park to Ann Morrison on a tube, with a shuttle bus back. The city treats it as summer transport.

title: Ski or ride Bald Mountain at Sun Valley
description: The first destination ski resort in America, and the chairlift was invented here in 1936 by an engineer who had been loading bananas onto ships.

title: Raft the Middle Fork of the Salmon
description: A hundred and sixty kilometres through the largest roadless area in the lower 48, with hot springs on the bank and permits by lottery.

title: Cycle the Trail of the Coeur d'Alenes
description: A hundred and twelve kilometres of paved former railway across the panhandle, laid over a mining superfund site that was capped beneath it.

title: Soak in a wild hot spring near Stanley
description: Boat Box is a steel tub on the riverbank you fill by bucket. Free, first come, and the Sawtooths are across the water.

title: Hear brass on Frenchmen Street
description: Three blocks of small rooms where the city actually goes to hear music, ten minutes' walk from Bourbon Street and nothing like it.

title: See the salt dome and the egret rookery at Avery Island
description: Tabasco has been made on the same salt dome since 1868, and the founder's son built a bird sanctuary that saved the snowy egret from plume hunters.

title: Walk under the Evangeline Oak in Cajun country
description: The Acadian deportation ended here for many families. The town still speaks Louisiana French in places and dances to it on Saturdays.

title: Go up the Louisiana State Capitol tower
description: The tallest state capitol in the country at 137 metres, built by Huey Long in fourteen months, who was shot in its corridor in 1935.

title: Eat crawfish at a boil in season
description: Boiled with corn, potato and enough cayenne to matter, tipped onto a newspaper table. Season runs roughly February to June.

title: Eat at the Portland working waterfront
description: A fishing pier that never turned into a theme, with the boats unloading beside the restaurants that buy from them.

title: Sail on a Maine windjammer
description: A fleet of restored nineteenth-century schooners that take passengers for several days with no engine and no fixed itinerary.

title: Climb Katahdin by the Knife Edge
description: The northern end of the Appalachian Trail. The Knife Edge is a metre wide in places with a long drop on both sides, and reservations are required.

title: Stand at the easternmost point in the United States
description: A candy-striped lighthouse at the first place in the country the sun touches, with whales in the Bay of Fundy offshore.

title: Look for moose at dawn near Moosehead Lake
description: Maine has the largest moose population in the lower 48. Dawn and dusk on the logging roads north of Greenville is where you see them.

title: See the Diego Rivera murals at the DIA
description: Twenty-seven panels on the Ford Rouge plant, painted 1932, that Rivera considered his best work. The city nearly sold them in bankruptcy.

title: Chase waterfalls to Tahquamenon
description: Root beer coloured from cedar tannin, sixty metres wide, and one of the largest falls east of the Mississippi.

title: Follow the Leelanau wine and cherry route
description: Lake Michigan moderates the peninsula enough to grow riesling, on ground that also produces most of the country's tart cherries.

title: Take the ferry to Isle Royale
description: The least visited national park in the lower 48, closed all winter, with a wolf and moose study running since 1958.

title: See the ice caves and frozen shore at Marquette
description: In a cold enough winter the spray freezes into curtains along the cliffs. Conditions change fast, so ask locally before walking on anything.

title: Cross the Stone Arch Bridge at St Anthony Falls
description: The only stone arch bridge on the whole Mississippi, built for the railway in 1883 and now for people. Free.

title: Paddle and camp in Voyageurs National Park
description: A park you can only really reach by water, on the fur trade route, with campsites accessible by boat alone.

title: Watch a laker come under the Aerial Lift Bridge
description: Thousand-foot ore carriers pass under a bridge that lifts in a minute. Arrival times are published, and the whole thing is free to watch.

title: Look into the Hull-Rust mine at Hibbing
description: Five kilometres long and 180 metres deep, the largest open pit iron mine in the world, and the town was moved to get at the ore.

title: Ride the coasters inside the Mall of America
description: An indoor theme park with roller coasters under a glass roof, which in a Minnesota January is a more reasonable idea than it sounds.

title: Walk Rowan Oak, where Faulkner wrote
description: His outline for A Fable is still pencilled on the study wall. The house is kept as he left it, in woods on the edge of town.

title: Take the boat to Ship Island
description: A barrier island twenty kilometres offshore with white sand, a Civil War fort, and no development of any kind.

title: See the two-room house Elvis was born in
description: Built by his father for 180 dollars. The scale of it is the thing that lands, more than anything at Graceland.

title: Eat hot tamales in the Mississippi Delta
description: A Delta tradition since Mexican labourers worked the cotton fields, sold from stands and simmered rather than steamed.

title: Walk the bluff and the antebellum houses at Natchez
description: More antebellum houses than anywhere in the South, on a bluff above the river, with the histories of the people who built them told alongside.

title: Wander the City Museum
description: A ten-storey former shoe factory turned into a climbable sculpture of salvage: aeroplanes on the roof, caves, and slides between floors.

title: See the caves under Silver Dollar City
description: The cathedral room is 61 metres high, and the theme park above it exists because the family needed to fund the cave tours.

title: Cycle the Katy Trail across Missouri
description: Three hundred and seventy kilometres of former railway, the longest developed rail trail in the country, much of it beside the Missouri River.

title: Scramble the granite at Elephant Rocks
description: Billion-year-old granite weathered into boulders the size of houses, with a braille trail built in 1972 that was among the first anywhere.

title: Swim in the blue water at Ha Ha Tonka
description: A collapsed cave system of sinkholes and natural bridges under the ruin of a castle a Kansas City businessman never finished.

title: Float the Clark Fork through Missoula
description: A town where people finish work and get in the river. There is a surf wave in Brennan's Wave right in the middle of it.

title: Drive the Bitterroot Valley to Lost Trail Pass
description: Lewis and Clark came through here half-starved in 1805. The mountains on the west side rise straight out of the valley floor.

title: Swim in Flathead Lake
description: The largest natural freshwater lake west of the Mississippi, clear enough to see the bottom at ten metres, and cold until late July.

title: See the Charles M Russell collection
description: The cowboy artist's own log studio stands beside the museum, and he painted the West from having actually worked in it.

title: Paddle or watch the Truckee River whitewater park
description: Eleven drop pools engineered through downtown Reno, free to use, with a wave that holds a kayak in place.

title: Swim at Sand Harbor on Lake Tahoe
description: Granite boulders and water clear to twenty metres on the Nevada shore, at 1,900 metres so it never gets warm.

title: Drive the ghost towns of the Nevada silver belt
description: Goldfield had 20,000 people in 1906 and has about 250 now, with the hotel, the courthouse and the school still standing on the highway.

title: See the Fly Geyser on a Friends of Black Rock walk
description: An accidental geyser from a 1964 drilling mishap, built up into mounds of red and green thermophile. Access is by booked walk only.

title: Ride the MS Mount Washington on Winnipesaukee
description: A 1888 route still run daily across the biggest lake in the state, calling at towns that have no road bridge between them.

title: Ride the Cannon Mountain tramway
description: The first aerial tramway in North America, opened 1938. The Old Man of the Mountain fell off this cliff in 2003 and is remembered below.

title: Climb Mount Monadnock
description: Among the most climbed mountains in the world, and a bare summit because farmers burned the trees off it twice in the 1800s.

title: Paddle Great Bay at high tide
description: An inland tidal estuary where half the water leaves twice a day, with oyster restoration beds and wintering eagles.

title: Board the USS North Carolina
description: A battleship you can go nine decks down inside, from the boiler rooms to the sick bay, with very little roped off.

title: Stand where the Wright brothers flew
description: Markers show all four flights of 17 December 1903. The first was twelve seconds and shorter than the wingspan of a 747.

title: Raft the Nantahala Gorge
description: Cold dam-release water through a gorge so narrow the sun reaches the bottom for only a few hours. Good for a first river.

title: Drive to the highest point east of the Mississippi
description: Two thousand and thirty-seven metres, with spruce-fir forest that belongs in Canada and weather to match. Free.

title: Ride the Cuyahoga Valley Scenic Railroad
description: A national park between Cleveland and Akron, with a train that will carry your bike one way so you ride the towpath back.

title: Walk the Great Serpent Mound
description: Four hundred and eleven metres of earthwork in the shape of a snake, on the rim of a meteor crater, aligned to the summer solstice sunset.

title: Take the ferry to Kelleys Island glacial grooves
description: The largest exposed glacial grooves in the world, gouged into limestone by ice eighteen thousand years ago.

title: Eat at the North Market
description: A public market since 1876, and where Jeni's ice cream started before it went national.

title: Ride the Duquesne Incline
description: An 1877 funicular up Mount Washington, still with its original wooden cars, to the view of the three rivers meeting.

title: Eat a cheesesteak and argue about where
description: Whiz, provolone or American, onions or not. The two famous places face each other across an intersection and neither is the local answer.

title: Drive the back roads of Lancaster County
description: The oldest Amish settlement in the country. Buggies use the shoulder, so pass slowly and wide, and nothing is open on a Sunday.

title: Walk to Bushkill Falls
description: Eight falls linked by boardwalk and stairs in a private glen that has charged admission since 1904 and kept the paths in good order.

title: Tour The Breakers
description: Seventy rooms built for the Vanderbilts in two years, with a great hall 15 metres high. The scale is the argument the Gilded Age was making.

title: Surf or watch the break at Narragansett Town Beach
description: The most consistent surf in New England, and one of the few town beaches in the country that charges walk-on admission.

title: Eat at Federal Hill
description: An Italian quarter with a pinecone hung over the entrance arch, and bakeries that have been in the same families for a century.

title: Walk out to Beavertail Light
description: The third oldest lighthouse site in the country on a rocky point, free, and the best storm-watching in the state.

title: Walk Huntington Beach and the alligator boardwalk
description: Considered the best birding on the coast, with a causeway where alligators lie a few metres from the road.

title: Walk the Falls Park suspension bridge
description: A four-lane bridge was demolished in 2002 to uncover the waterfall it had been hiding, and a curved footbridge put over it instead.

title: Walk the boneyard beach at Botany Bay
description: Dead oaks and palmettos standing in the surf where the sea has taken the land. Free, closed Tuesdays, and you may take nothing off the beach.

title: Climb Table Rock in the upcountry
description: Twelve kilometres return and 640 metres of climb up a granite dome, with the Blue Ridge escarpment laid out at the top.

title: Drive the Needles Highway
description: Granite spires and tunnels cut so tight that buses cannot pass. It was called impossible before it was built in 1922.

title: Go down into Wind Cave
description: One of the longest caves in the world and the densest known boxwork formation anywhere, under prairie with bison on top.

title: Walk the falls in the middle of Sioux Falls
description: Seven thousand litres a second over pink quartzite in the middle of the city, with the ruins of a 1881 mill beside it. Free.

title: See the Crazy Horse Memorial in progress
description: Begun in 1948, still unfinished, and funded without government money by choice. The face alone is larger than all of Rushmore.

title: Paddle the Missouri National Recreational River
description: One of the last stretches of the Missouri still braiding across sandbars the way Lewis and Clark described it.

title: Ride the Incline Railway up Lookout Mountain
description: A 72.7 per cent grade at the top, which is about as steep as a passenger railway gets anywhere.

title: Eat dry-rub ribs in Memphis
description: Memphis argues for dry rub where the rest of the South argues for sauce, and the barbecue contest each May is taken very seriously.

title: Walk to the Fiery Gizzard trail bluffs
description: Regularly named among the toughest and best day hikes in the east, through boulder fields and hemlock gorge on the plateau rim.

title: Drive the Bighorn Scenic Byway
description: A range Yellowstone traffic drives straight past, with a medicine wheel at 2,900 metres built by Plains peoples and still in use.

title: Soak in the free state bath at Thermopolis
description: The 1896 treaty transferring the spring required that some of it stay free to everyone forever, and the state still honours it.

title: Watch a rodeo in Wyoming
description: Small-town rodeo is a working sport here rather than a show, and the July nights in Sheridan and Cody are when to see it.
